_readme: Channel definitions for kawasaki_logger.py. You can edit these in the app's Channels tab.
pid: hex local identifier sent as '21 <pid>'. every: read on every Nth update (1 = every time).
formula variables: A B C D... (data bytes), raw, sraw, n, d. Functions: abs min max round signed(v,bits) math.*
verified: set true once a channel's scaling has been checked against a known-good reading.
gauge_min / gauge_max: range of the tile's gauge bar. null = scale to the values seen this session.

priority: iOS app only. true gives this channel a dedicated re-read on every other poll cycle (see OBDEngine.pollStep), for gauges that need to track faster than 'every' alone allows. Defaults to false; not used by the Windows app.

pids.name: Engine RPM
pids.notes: Was 'raw' with no scaling (unverified default). At base idle on a 2007 Ultra LX, raw read 306 while the ski's actual idle is ~1200 rpm — 306 * 4 = 1224, a close match. This ECU appears to store RPM in units of 4 rpm per count (opposite of standard OBD-II's PID 0x0C, which divides by 4). Confirmed at one data point (idle); would be good to confirm at a second RPM (e.g. a brief rev) to rule out a non-multiplicative offset.

pids.name: Throttle sensor
pids.notes: Ultra LX: closed = 246 and wide open = 912 counts (about 1.2 V and 4.5 V if 10-bit at 5 V). Use Capture 0 % / 100 % in Edit to set your own ski's values.

pids.name: Intake Pressure
pids.notes: This ski has only one physical pressure sensor (in the intake manifold) — no separate barometric sensor. PID 0x05 is that live reading: in a 2026-10-13 idle/rev research log it read ~101.7 kPa at key-on/engine-off (atmospheric), dropped to ~58 kPa once the engine started and settled into idle (manifold vacuum), then rose to ~79 kPa during a rev to 4284 rpm (vacuum partially collapsing). PID 0x08 previously held this channel but was found frozen at a constant 101.8 kPa for the entire session regardless of engine/RPM state — a dead/duplicate register — and was removed. every bumped from 10 to 1 since this is a fast-changing signal, not a slow one like true barometric pressure.

pids.name: Engine temp
pids.notes: Reads degrees C plus 40 (62 = 22 C = 72 F in a 70 F garage). One point only: check against an infrared thermometer once it's warm. Units of C make it switchable between C and F. Seen on a 2007 Ultra LX with key on and engine off. Check on your own ski. A 2026-10-13 water test on another ski showed this channel staying a sane 59-70 C through a sustained 6000+ rpm run while that ski threw an OILH (oil temp high) warning — so on that ECU at least, 0x06 is not the oil sensor; see PID 0x98 below.

pids.name: Intake air temp
pids.notes: Same encoding as engine temp. Seen on a 2007 Ultra LX with key on and engine off. Check on your own ski.

pids.name: Oil Temp
pids.notes: Found via the full-scan Research Log, not in the original kline.py defaults. In a 2026-10-13 water test, this ski threw an OILH (oil temp high) dash warning and backed off from a sustained ~6200 rpm / 42 mph cruise to idle at t=117s, never recovering for the rest of the session. PID 0x98, decoded with the same raw-40 convention as 0x06/0x07, climbed 142C -> 135C -> 153C over that same run, peaking right as the warning apparently hit — while 0x06 ('Engine temp') stayed a boring 59-70C the whole time. Also at t=116.8s, PID 0x02 flipped one bit (0x40->0x42 in its first byte) and latched there for the rest of the session, which looks like a fault/status flag turning on at the same moment. Strong circumstantial case for 0x98 = oil temperature, but unverified — confirm with an infrared thermometer at the oil tank/cooler next time OILH comes on, watching this channel live.

pids.name: Battery
pids.notes: Switched off: PID 0x0A returned 00 00 on an Ultra LX with key on, so it isn't battery voltage there. A 2026-10-13 idle/rev research log on another ski showed 0x0A holding a constant raw value (664) from when it first responded all the way through engine shutoff, with zero sag — a real battery would drop once the alternator stops charging, so 0x0A likely isn't voltage there either. Use the PID scanner to find the right one (look for a value that jumps up when the engine runs and sags after shutoff).
